Marketing Campaigns: EDA and Hypothesis Testing¶

Course: Applied Data Science with Python (course-end project)

Objective: explore the factors that drive customer acquisition using the four Ps of the marketing mix (People, Product, Place, Promotion), clean and engineer the data, and test four business hypotheses on marketing_data.csv.

The raw import exposes two problems: the income column is named ' Income ' (leading and trailing spaces) and is read as text because values look like $84,835.00; Dt_Customer is also text (m/d/yy). Both are fixed below.

Only Income has missing values (24 rows). Before grouping, the categorical labels need cleaning:

  • Education: 2n Cycle is the European label for a Master's degree, so it is merged with Master.
  • Marital_Status: Alone is Single; YOLO and Absurd are not real statuses (5 rows in total) so they are mapped to Single as the closest neutral category. Together (partnered, unmarried) is kept distinct from Married.

# impute with the median income of customers sharing Education + Marital_Status (median is robust to the income outlier)
n_missing = int(df['Income'].isna().sum())
df['Income'] = df['Income'].fillna(grp.transform('median'))
print('Missing before:', n_missing, '| after:', df['Income'].isna().sum())
METRICS['income_missing_imputed'] = n_missing

Missing before: 24 | after: 0

Median imputation by (Education, Marital_Status) fills the gaps (the printed count after imputation should be 0). The median is preferred over the mean because there is a very large income outlier (see Step 5).

Step 5. Box plots and histograms, outlier treatment¶

In [9]:
num_cols = ['Age','Income','Total_Spending','Total_Purchases','Recency','NumWebVisitsMonth']
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, len(num_cols), figsize=(20, 7))
for i, c in enumerate(num_cols):
    sns.boxplot(y=df[c], ax=ax[0, i], color='#4C72B0'); ax[0, i].set_title(f'{c} (box)')
    sns.histplot(df[c], kde=True, ax=ax[1, i], color='#4C72B0'); ax[1, i].set_title(f'{c} (hist)')
save('01_distributions_before')
In [10]:
def iqr_bounds(s):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75]); i = q3 - q1
    return q1 - 1.5*i, q3 + 1.5*i
rows = []
for c in num_cols + ['MntWines','MntMeatProducts','MntGoldProds','NumDealsPurchases']:
    lo, hi = iqr_bounds(df[c]); rows.append([c, lo, hi, int(((df[c] < lo) | (df[c] > hi)).sum())])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['variable','lower_fence','upper_fence','n_outliers']).set_index('variable').round(1)
Out[10]:
lower_fence upper_fence n_outliers
variable
Age 10.0 82.0 3
Income -13587.8 117416.2 8
Total_Spending -1396.4 2510.6 3
Total_Purchases -12.0 36.0 0
Recency -51.0 149.0 0
NumWebVisitsMonth -3.0 13.0 8
MntWines -697.0 1225.0 35
MntMeatProducts -308.0 556.0 175
MntGoldProds -61.5 126.5 207
NumDealsPurchases -2.0 6.0 86

Findings: Age has implausible values (very old birth years give an age over 100), Income has an extreme value far above the next largest, and spending / purchase counts are right skewed with a long tail of heavy buyers.

Treatment:

  • Age and Income contain errors or extreme values that distort means and correlations, so they are winsorised (capped) at the IQR fences. Capping keeps the rows, which matters because they carry valid purchase data.
  • Spending and purchase counts are right skewed but the high values are genuine heavy-buying customers; capping them would erase the very top-performers the analysis is looking for, so they are left unchanged.
In [11]:
before = df[['Age','Income']].describe().loc[['min','max','mean']]
for c in ['Age','Income']:
    lo, hi = iqr_bounds(df[c]); n = int(((df[c] < lo) | (df[c] > hi)).sum())
    df[c] = df[c].clip(lo, hi); METRICS[f'{c.lower()}_outliers_capped'] = n
    print(f'{c}: capped {n} values to [{lo:.0f}, {hi:.0f}]')
print(pd.concat([before.add_suffix(' (before)'), df[['Age','Income']].describe().loc[['min','max','mean']].add_suffix(' (after)')], axis=1).round(1))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7))
for i, c in enumerate(['Age','Income']):
    sns.boxplot(y=df[c], ax=ax[0, i], color='#55A868'); ax[0, i].set_title(f'{c} after capping')
    sns.histplot(df[c], kde=True, ax=ax[1, i], color='#55A868')
save('02_distributions_after_capping')

Step 6. Encoding: ordinal and one-hot¶

In [12]:
# Education is ordered -> ordinal encoding; Marital_Status and Country are unordered -> one-hot

dfe = df.copy()
dfe['Education_Ord'] = dfe['Education'].map(edu_order)
dfe = pd.get_dummies(dfe, columns=['Marital_Status', 'Country'], prefix=['Marital', 'Country'], dtype=int)
print(dfe.shape)
dfe.filter(regex='^(Education|Marital_|Country_)').head()

Step 8. Hypothesis tests¶

All tests use a 5% significance level. Welch's t-test is used for group means (no equal-variance assumption), with a Mann-Whitney U check because the purchase counts are not normal.

H1. Older customers lean toward in-store shopping¶

In [14]:
# 'older' = age 55+; metric = share of purchases made in store
df['Store_Share'] = df['NumStorePurchases'] / df['Total_Purchases'].replace(0, np.nan)
older = df.loc[df['Age'] >= 55, 'Store_Share'].dropna(); younger = df.loc[df['Age'] < 55, 'Store_Share'].dropna()
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(older, younger, equal_var=False, alternative='greater')
u, pu = stats.mannwhitneyu(older, younger, alternative='greater')
print(f'n older={len(older)}, n younger={len(younger)}')
print(f'mean store share: older={older.mean():.3f}, younger={younger.mean():.3f}')
print(f'Welch t={t:.3f}, p={p:.4g} | Mann-Whitney p={pu:.4g}')
m = df.Total_Purchases > 0
r, pr = stats.pearsonr(df.loc[m, 'Age'], df.loc[m, 'Store_Share'])
print(f'Pearson r(age, store share)={r:.3f}, p={pr:.4g}')
METRICS['H1_p'] = float(p); METRICS['H1_older_store_share'] = float(older.mean()); METRICS['H1_younger_store_share'] = float(younger.mean())
sns.boxplot(data=df.assign(Group=np.where(df.Age >= 55, '55+', 'under 55')), x='Group', y='Store_Share'); plt.title('Share of purchases made in store by age group')
save('04_h1_age_store')
print('Reject H0: older customers shop more in store' if p < .05 else 'Fail to reject H0')

n older=569, n younger=1665
mean store share: older=0.485, younger=0.512
Welch t=-3.790, p=0.9999 | Mann-Whitney p=1
Pearson r(age, store share)=-0.105, p=5.991e-07

Fail to reject H0

Interpretation: if the one-sided p-value above is below 0.05, customers aged 55 and over make a larger share of their purchases in store than younger customers, supporting H1; the printed means show the size of the gap. Age 55 is an assumed cut-off for "older".

Result: the hypothesis is not supported. Customers aged 55+ have a slightly lower store share (0.485) than younger customers (0.512), the one-sided p-value is about 1, and the age/store-share correlation is weakly negative (r = -0.105). The two-sided effect is small.

H2. Customers with children favour online shopping¶

In [15]:
kids = df['Total_Children'] > 0
df['Web_Share'] = df['NumWebPurchases'] / df['Total_Purchases'].replace(0, np.nan)
for metric in ['NumWebPurchases', 'Web_Share']:
    a = df.loc[kids, metric].dropna(); b = df.loc[~kids, metric].dropna()
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False, alternative='greater')
    u, pu = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative='greater')
    print(f'{metric}: with children mean={a.mean():.3f} (n={len(a)}), without={b.mean():.3f} (n={len(b)}) | Welch p={p:.4g} (one-sided, children > none) | MWU p={pu:.4g}')
    METRICS['H2_p_' + ('web_share' if metric == 'Web_Share' else 'web_count')] = float(p)
print('Web visits per month:', df.groupby(kids)['NumWebVisitsMonth'].mean().round(2).to_dict())
g = df.assign(Has_Children=np.where(kids, 'Has children', 'No children'))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
sns.barplot(data=g, x='Has_Children', y='Web_Share', ax=ax[0]); ax[0].set_title('Web share of purchases')
sns.barplot(data=g, x='Has_Children', y='NumWebPurchases', ax=ax[1]); ax[1].set_title('Web purchases per customer')
save('05_h2_children_web')

NumWebPurchases: with children mean=3.962 (n=1602), without=4.393 (n=638) | Welch p=0.9998 (one-sided, children > none) | MWU p=1
Web_Share: with children mean=0.353 (n=1600), without=0.273 (n=634) | Welch p=1.089e-46 (one-sided, children > none) | MWU p=7.407e-53
Web visits per month: {False: 3.48, True: 6.05}

Interpretation: two views are tested. The count test asks whether parents buy more online in absolute terms; the share test asks whether a bigger fraction of their purchases is online, which is closer to the "convenience" argument.

Result: parents buy slightly fewer web purchases in absolute terms (3.96 vs 4.39; hypothesis not supported on counts), but web purchases are a significantly larger share of their purchases (0.353 vs 0.273, p far below 0.05) and they also visit the website more (6.05 vs 3.48 visits per month). So the convenience argument is supported for channel mix, not for purchase volume.

H3. Store sales may be cannibalised by other channels¶

In [16]:
res = []
for ch in ['NumWebPurchases', 'NumCatalogPurchases']:
    r, p = stats.pearsonr(df['NumStorePurchases'], df[ch]); rs, ps = stats.spearmanr(df['NumStorePurchases'], df[ch])
    res.append([ch, r, p, rs, ps])
other = df['NumWebPurchases'] + df['NumCatalogPurchases']
r, p = stats.pearsonr(df['NumStorePurchases'], other); rs, ps = stats.spearmanr(df['NumStorePurchases'], other)
res.append(['Web+Catalog', r, p, rs, ps])
h3 = pd.DataFrame(res, columns=['vs store purchases','pearson_r','pearson_p','spearman_rho','spearman_p']).round(4); print(h3)
METRICS['H3_r_store_vs_web'] = float(res[0][1]); METRICS['H3_r_store_vs_catalog'] = float(res[1][1])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
sns.regplot(data=df, x='NumStorePurchases', y='NumWebPurchases', ax=ax[0], scatter_kws={'alpha': .3}, line_kws={'color': 'red'})
sns.regplot(data=df, x='NumStorePurchases', y='NumCatalogPurchases', ax=ax[1], scatter_kws={'alpha': .3}, line_kws={'color': 'red'})
save('06_h3_cannibalisation')

    vs store purchases  pearson_r  pearson_p  spearman_rho  spearman_p
0      NumWebPurchases     0.5027        0.0        0.6726         0.0
1  NumCatalogPurchases     0.5187        0.0        0.7086         0.0
2          Web+Catalog     0.6154        0.0        0.7375         0.0

Interpretation: cannibalisation would show up as a negative correlation between store purchases and web/catalog purchases. Check the signs of the coefficients above: positive correlations mean customers who buy more in store also buy more through other channels, i.e. the channels complement rather than replace each other.

Result: store purchases correlate positively with web (r = 0.50) and catalog (r = 0.52) purchases, so there is no evidence of cannibalisation. A cross-customer correlation cannot rule out substitution within a single customer.

H4. Does the United States outperform the rest of the world in total purchases?¶

In [17]:
us = df.loc[df.Country == 'US', 'Total_Purchases']; row = df.loc[df.Country != 'US', 'Total_Purchases']
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(us, row, equal_var=False, alternative='greater'); u, pu = stats.mannwhitneyu(us, row, alternative='greater')
t2, p2 = stats.ttest_ind(us, row, equal_var=False)
print(f'US mean={us.mean():.2f} (n={len(us)}), rest of world mean={row.mean():.2f} (n={len(row)})')
print(f'One-sided (US > rest): Welch t={t:.3f}, p={p:.4g}; Mann-Whitney p={pu:.4g}')
print(f'Two-sided Welch p={p2:.4g}')
METRICS['H4_p'] = float(p); METRICS['H4_us_mean'] = float(us.mean()); METRICS['H4_row_mean'] = float(row.mean())
print(df.groupby('Country')['Total_Purchases'].agg(['count','mean','sum']).round(2).sort_values('mean', ascending=False))
sns.barplot(data=df, x='Country', y='Total_Purchases', order=df.groupby('Country')['Total_Purchases'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
plt.title('Mean total purchases per customer by country'); save('07_h4_us_vs_world')

Result: US mean 13.51 vs 12.49 for the rest of the world; one-sided p = 0.072 (two-sided 0.145). The US is nominally higher but not significantly so at the 5% level.

            complainers  share_of_complainers_%  share_of_all_customers_%
Education                                                                
Basic                 0                     0.0                       2.4

Complaints are rare. Compare each education level's share of complainers with its share of all customers: a level that complains in proportion to its size shows no particular dissatisfaction. The group is small, so conclusions are tentative.

Result: 21 customers complained (0.94%): 14 Graduation, 6 Master, 1 PhD, none Basic. Graduation is slightly over-represented (66.7% of complainers vs 50.3% of customers) and PhD under-represented (4.8% vs 21.7%), but with 21 cases this is tentative.

Conclusions¶

  • Data quality: income was text in a $ format with missing values (imputed with Education x Marital-status medians); category labels (2n Cycle, Alone, YOLO, Absurd) were cleaned; Age and Income outliers were capped.
  • Products: wine (about 50%) and meat (28%) dominate revenue; fruits, sweets and fish are small.
  • Hypotheses: H1 (older prefer store) not supported; H2 supported for web share but not web count; H3 no cannibalisation (positive correlations); H4 US not significantly higher (p = 0.072).
  • Families: spending falls sharply as children at home increase; age does not predict campaign acceptance; Spain has the most accepters.
  • Limits: the data is a single cross-section, correlation is not causation, the "older" cut-off (55) is an assumption, and some groups (US, complainers) are small.
